message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• The Texas Property Code §92.001 requires landlords to maintain the property in a habitable condition. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to fix a serious issue, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but do so carefully and document everything. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Notice must specify the date, time, and purpose. | • Ask for a written notice if you’re unsure. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing laws, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a written notice of non‑renewal at least 30 days before the lease ends. | • Keep a copy of any notice you receive. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the formal eviction process: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights group or attorney. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to repair a problem and deduct the cost from rent if the landlord fails to act within a reasonable time. | • Document the issue, send a written notice, keep receipts, and calculate the deduction carefully. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to use the premises without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any disturbances (e.g., excessive noise, harassment) in writing. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot enter your unit without proper notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in writing. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide insurance for your personal property. | • Consider renter’s insurance. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) provides tenant‑rights information.
• Local tenant‑rights organizations (e.g., Texas Tenants Union).
• Legal aid clinics. | • Use these resources for disputes or questions. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand rent amount, due dates, pet policies, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for lease termination. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Send written notices for repairs; keep copies. 5. **Keep Records of Payments** – Bank statements, receipts, or online payment confirmations. 6. **Seek Help Early** – If you face eviction or discrimination, contact a tenant‑rights group or attorney. --- #### When to Call a Lawyer - You receive an eviction notice and need to contest it. - You suspect unlawful discrimination. - You’re unsure whether a repair and deduct claim is permissible. - You want to negotiate lease terms or amendments. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. For personalized guidance, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
